Curriculum Vitae (PDF) →

I build open-source MRI acquisition and reconstruction methods — with a focus on diffusion MRI that behaves the same on any scanner, from any vendor.

My research develops vendor-agnostic pulse sequences and reconstruction pipelines that reduce inter-scanner variability in diffusion MRI, so that multi-center neuroimaging studies can trust that a measurement means the same thing whether it was acquired on a Siemens, GE, Philips, or Bruker system. I work across the full imaging chain: sequence design in Pulseq, high-resolution and super-resolution acquisition, and learning-based reconstruction and denoising.

I am a Ph.D. candidate at Northeastern University, advised by Dr. Deniz Erdogmus, and co-advised by Dr. Yogesh Rathi at Harvard Medical School, where I work at the Brigham and Women's Hospital.

Research Directions

Vendor-agnostic dMRI
Reproducible diffusion MRI across scanners. Open-source Pulseq sequences that cut cross-scanner variability in FA and diffusivity for multi-center studies.
Super-resolution
Mesoscale whole-brain imaging. Rotating-view and implicit-neural-representation reconstruction for high-isotropic-resolution imaging in clinically feasible scan times.
Reconstruction
Consistent, scanner-adaptive pipelines. Unified reconstruction and coil-level denoising that preserve microstructure while removing scanner-specific noise.
Sequence design
Accelerated relaxation–diffusion. Multi-echo and time-division-multiplexing sequences for unbiased T2 and relaxation-diffusion measurement.
